The Covenant of Abraham is the foundational agreement between God and Abraham in Jewish tradition. It establishes Abraham as the father of a chosen people and promises his descendants would multiply, inherit the land of Canaan, and serve God. Sealed by the rite of circumcision, this covenant became the legal and spiritual basis for Jewish identity and practice. According to Genesis, God promised Abraham that his descendants would be as numerous as the stars and would inherit Canaan as an eternal possession. The covenant was formally sealed through circumcision, which became the sign of the covenant inscribed on the male body of every Jewish male child. God changed Abram's name to Abraham, meaning "father of multitudes," to reflect the covenant's promise, and his wife Sarai became Sarah, meaning "princess." The covenant passed to Abraham's son Isaac, the child of promise, rather than Ishmael, establishing the line of descent through the promised son. Circumcision, called brit milah, on the eighth day of a male child's life ritualizes entry into the covenant community and remains a central Jewish practice. The covenant emphasized God's unconditional grace rather than human merit, establishing the principle that Israel's chosenness derived from divine favor, not earned righteousness.
